source.title: Semantics or spelling? Probing contextual word embeddings with orthographic noise
source.authors: Jacob A. Matthews; John R. Starr; Marten van Schijndel

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how a single model's word representation changes when its input word is edited. It does not measure alignment or convergence between independently trained models, so it does not test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported comparisons are between clean and character-edited words within a model, not between models' representations of the same data. They are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. The paper also reports tokenizer distributions, which are not rows because they do not measure representational similarity.
record.test_reason: The study compares a single model's representation of a clean word with its representation of the same word after a one-character edit. It never compares representations across models, seeds or modalities, so it neither tests nor uses any version of the convergence claim. It does not cite the original sources either; it bears on the topic only loosely, through its point that similarity measures such as cosine are fragile. Relation 'discusses' overstates the link. Strictly, 'cites_only' is also inaccurate because the sources are not cited, but it is the closest available category for a study that does not engage the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that CWEs are highly sensitive to single-character noise, and more so for words made of fewer tokens. They conclude that CWEs may not be reliable semantic proxies and that representational similarity should be interpreted with caution.
record.recipe_differences: The study probes within-model sensitivity to character edits; it does not apply a method for measuring inter-model convergence.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity results vary with the metric (cosine versus Spearman), context availability, and original word token length. Context notably increases similarity for some BERT and XLNet models but has almost no effect for BLOOM, RoBERTa, and larger GPT-2 variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean-pooled last-layer word embeddings from 11 PLMs change substantially when a single character of the word is edited. Spearman similarity between clean and edited versions is about 0.2–0.5 for single-token words, with or without context. Cosine stays near 1.0 for BLOOM, GPT2-small and RoBERTa, so the conclusion depends on the metric. Context helps BERT and XLNet but barely helps BLOOM, RoBERTa or the larger GPT-2 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model contextual word representations are sensitive to minimal orthographic noise in a way tied to subword tokenization. Cosine similarity can mask this sensitivity because of anisotropy and rogue dimensions.

record.problems: The authors note reliance on third-party packages and open-source models, use of only last-layer mean pooling, a Wikitext vocabulary that may not represent English words in all contexts, random-character edits that may not reflect natural noise, and exclusion of words with three or fewer characters. Many model-specific values are shown in figures rather than stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Individual per-model and per-token-length figure values are not separately extracted from Figures 3 and 4; they are presented only graphically, while the text-level aggregate findings are recorded above.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ["none"]. R9 is the authors' interpretation (40–60% of semantic identity lost) rather than a separate measurement, and could be merged with R5. The metric dependence (cosine versus Spearman) is a within-model observation and should not be credited to V6, which concerns similarity measured between models.

rows.subject: All tested PLMs (aggregate result as reported)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean-pooled representations of clean and single-character-edited words without context using Spearman correlation.

conditions.value: alphabetic words over 3 characters from Wikitext-2-raw-v1

rows.measure: Spearman rank correlation between each clean word representation and its edited counterpart
rows.uncertainty: 99% confidence intervals shown in Figure 1; exact interval values not stated
rows.note: The text reports this range for single-token words and says standardized similarities are low across models except at the highest token lengths.

rows.subject: BLOOM (bloom-560m)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean-pooled representations of clean and single-character-edited words without context using cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between clean and edited word representations
rows.uncertainty: 99% confidence intervals shown in Figure 1; exact interval values not stated
rows.note: The text names BLOOM among the models with average cosine similarities close to 1.0 for all token lengths.

rows.subject: GPT-2 (gpt2)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean-pooled representations of clean and single-character-edited words without context using cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between clean and edited word representations
rows.uncertainty: 99% confidence intervals shown in Figure 1; exact interval values not stated
rows.note: The text calls this model GPT2-small and names it among the models with average cosine similarities close to 1.0 for all token lengths.

rows.subject: All tested PLMs (aggregate result as reported)
rows.operation_detail: Compared similarity of clean and single-character-edited word representations across original-word token lengths.

rows.value: Words represented by fewer tokens are more sensitive; similarity approaches 1.0 at high token lengths
rows.uncertainty: 99% confidence intervals shown in figures; exact interval values not stated
rows.note: The paper explicitly describes token length as associated with noise sensitivity; it does not report this as inter-model convergence.

rows.operation_detail: Interpreted similarity of clean and single-character-edited word representations in context as retained word semantic identity.

rows.value: 40%-60% of a word's semantic identity is lost when a single character is changed
rows.note: This is the authors' summary interpretation of their within-model noise comparison, not a measurement of alignment between models.
